item.title: FTA concerned by three teacher deaths
item.description: THE Fiji Teachers Association (FTA) is raising concerns over the health and wellbeing of teachers following the deaths of three members last week. FTA general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga said the association was increasingly dealing with cases of teachers dying at a young age, while two members were currently in India receiving medical treatment funded by the association.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Teachers Association (FTA) is raising concerns over the health and wellbeing of teachers following the deaths of three members last week.

FTA general secretary Paula Manumanunitoga said the association was increasingly dealing with cases of teachers dying at a young age, while two members were currently in India receiving medical treatment funded by the association.

“Last week we had three deaths, all members of FTA,” he said.

The association provides financial assistance to members facing serious illnesses, including overseas treatment and medical evacuation.

“We provide $40,000 to a member that needs medical evacuation. All his medical expenses are paid for, his airfare, and for an aid to somebody to go with him.”

FTA also provides a $7000 funeral insurance payout to families of deceased members.

However, he said the growing demand for medical and welfare assistance was putting pressure on the association’s funds.

FTA members contribute $10 every fortnight, amounting to $260 annually.

Mr Manumanunitoga urged teachers to prioritise their health by attending regular medical checks and reducing excessive yaqona, alcohol and tobacco consumption.

He said while the FTA remained committed to supporting members and their families during times of illness and hardship, the recent deaths highlighted the need for early medical attention and healthier lifestyles.

item.title: Navua declared a town
item.description: AFTER more than five decades of waiting, Navua’s long-held dream of becoming a town has finally become a reality, with Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka yesterday declaring it Fiji’s 12th town and 14th municipality. item.content:encoded:
AFTER more than five decades of waiting, Navua’s long-held dream of becoming a town has finally become a reality, with Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka yesterday declaring it Fiji’s 12th town and 14th municipality.

Speaking at the ceremony, Mr Rabuka said the declaration marked the fulfilment of an aspiration that dated back to 1973 and recognised generations of people who had contributed to the development of Navua.

He said after many years of advocacy, conservation and preparation, the people of Navua had the privilege of seeing that long-held hope becoming a reality.

Permanent secretary for Local Government Seema Sharma said the declaration was particularly significant for the ministry because Fiji had not established a new town for 16 years, the last being declared in 2010.

Mr Rabuka said the declaration was not an end in itself and warned that the new status brought greater responsibilities for the council, businesses, communities and residents.

He said the transition must be guided by good governance, financial responsibility, effective planning and accountability.

Mr Rabuka said Navua’s growth must also be carefully managed to prevent pressure on roads, drainage, water and sanitation systems.

He highlighted the need for stronger resilience against flooding, cyclones and heavy rainfall, while protecting the Navua River and surrounding environment.

He said the true measure of yesterday’s historic declaration will be what Navua delivers for its people.

“The real meaning of today will be seen in what comes next.”

item.title: Wailea residents reject waste blame
item.description: RESIDENTS living near the Wailea St bridge in Vatuwaqa, Suva, have rejected claims they were responsible for the large amount of rubbish trapped by a trashboom in the creek. The rubbish has accumulated around the Trashboom Pacific installation, creating foul odours and raising health concerns for nearby residents.
item.content:encoded:
RESIDENTS living near the Wailea St bridge in Vatuwaqa, Suva, have rejected claims they were responsible for the large amount of rubbish trapped by a trashboom in the creek.

The rubbish has accumulated around the Trashboom Pacific installation, creating foul odours and raising health concerns for nearby residents.

The issue came into focus after The Fiji Times posted a video on Thursday showing the trash boom heavily laden with rubbish.

Minister for Environment and Climate Change Lynda Tabuya subsequently called on residents of Wailea and surrounding communities to take responsibility for keeping the area clean.

“Stop dumping rubbish into the river in the first place,” she said.

“The trashboom did not create this rubbish. You did. But 23-year-old Wailea resident Jioji Nasaya, who lives near the trashboom, disputed the claim.

“Why would we throw rubbish into the creek when we know it will be trapped by the trashboom and ultimately affect us,” Mr Nasaya said.

He said rubbish was coming from upstream, flowing from Samabula through Nabua and eventually into Wailea.

Resident Tomasi Tuabua, 60, said much of the rubbish was washed downstream during heavy rain.

“The rubbish problem in this creek has existed for years. It is good to see the trashboom helping to prevent the waste from flowing into the sea. It just needs to be cleaned.”

Meanwhile, Trashboom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said the rubbish could not be safely removed because a Water Authority of Fiji sewer line was discharging directly around the boom.

Questions sent to WAF about the sewer leak remained unanswered.

item.title: Cleaners face toxic rubbish – Needles, glue cans found
item.description: USED needles and cans of glue are among the dangerous items being pulled from Fiji’s waterways by workers clearing trashboom sites, raising serious concerns about the hazards faced by those removing rubbish. Trashboom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said workers were regularly finding discarded needles and glue cans mixed with other waste trapped by the booms.
item.content:encoded:
USED needles and cans of glue are among the dangerous items being pulled from Fiji’s waterways by workers clearing trashboom sites, raising serious concerns about the hazards faced by those removing rubbish.

Trashboom Pacific director Wayne Fuakilau said workers were regularly finding discarded needles and glue cans mixed with other waste trapped by the booms.

“In one site we can intercept three to four needles and two to three cans of glue,” Mr Fuakilau said.

He said the public often saw a boom filled with rubbish but did not see the risks workers faced when removing and analysing its contents.

“People will see a full boom, but they don’t see what we go through when we collect and analyse data.”

Mr Fuakilau said workers had to exercise extreme caution when sorting the rubbish because of the presence of needles.

“And we have to really be careful sorting because of the needles.”

The discarded items are removed and disposed of through respective municipal council skip bins, which Mr Fuakilau said were then taken to landfill.

But he warned of the potential environmental and public health consequences if such hazardous waste was not intercepted.

“Imagine those needles and glue cans ending up in the mangroves for the crabs.”

Mr Fuakilau said the safety of his team remained a major concern as the company expanded its work to intercept rubbish before it reached the ocean.

“So not only there’s leaking sewer, there’s needles as well that we have to be aware of.”

item.title: Plan for protest march
item.description: RESIDENTS of Simla in Lautoka are gearing up for a peaceful protest march and potential legal action following a controversial decision to rezone a residential area for a new shopping mall, says Lautoka Residents and Ratepayers Association president Narayan Reddy. The said property is located at Covuli St, Lautoka.
item.content:encoded:
RESIDENTS of Simla in Lautoka are gearing up for a peaceful protest march and potential legal action following a controversial decision to rezone a residential area for a new shopping mall, says Lautoka Residents and Ratepayers Association president Narayan Reddy.

The said property is located at Covuli St, Lautoka.

Mr Reddy said many were concerned over procedural irregularities and a severe lack of transparency via a comprehensive consultation.

“An initial application to convert the residential land to commercial use was firmly rejected by both the Lautoka City Council and the Department of Town and Country Planning,” he said.

“Despite this rejection, the council published an advertisement claiming the commercial rezoning had received full approval from both authorities.”

Under standard regulations, Mr Reddy said bypassing a formal appeal process involving the council, the department, and an independent tribunal was prohibited.

“When the association requested a written explanation, the special administrator failed to provide a formal response. Instead, he made phone calls claiming the decision rested solely with the Department of Town Country and Planning, contradicting the council’s own public notice.”

Mr Reddy said the project sat directly adjacent to the city centre making the construction of the proposed shopping mall unnecessary

“The community is taking a stand because of unanswered questions and a general lack of accountability from authorities.

“We consider this rezoning process unlawful and are fully prepared to take the matter further, including pursuing legal action in court if necessary.”

Lautoka Board of Special Administrators chair Taitusi Rasoki said the council could only facilitate the planning of the project, however, it was not at liberty to approve the project.

Mr Rasoki referred further queries regarding the project to the Department of Town and Country Planning.

Questions sent to Director of Town and Country Planning Mohammed Ziar regarding the concerns raised remain unanswered.

item.title: Find a balance to retain enough skilled workforce – Smirk
item.description: A PROSPEROUS Fijian economy could be one where remittances play a much smaller role in the economy. Westpac Australia senior economist Justin Smirk shared this at the Fiji-Australia Business Council Forum noting that a reduction in remittances could signal that Fiji had created an economy capable of retaining more of its workforce and providing opportunities for people to earn sustainable incomes
item.content:encoded:
A PROSPEROUS Fijian economy could be one where remittances play a much smaller role in the economy.

Westpac Australia senior economist Justin Smirk shared this at the Fiji-Australia Business Council Forum noting that a reduction in remittances could signal that Fiji had created an economy capable of retaining more of its workforce and providing opportunities for people to earn sustainable incomes at home.

Speaking at the forum, Mr Smirk said Fiji had the foundations needed to generate growth, but needed to consider how its resilience could be transformed into long-term prosperity.

Mr Smirk highlighted Fiji’s relatively low labour force participation, saying this was important given the country’s level of debt.

“Participation determines how many people were working, earning incomes and paying taxes, which in turn supports the Government’s ability to manage its finances,” he said.

“If you want to continue to run large deficits, we have to think about ways that we can improve our participation.”

He also pointed to Fiji’s heavy reliance on remittances, saying they presented a risk because they reflected Fijians working offshore and represented a loss of talent from the domestic economy.

“I think some level of migration and brain drain is inevitable for smaller economies. You know, Fiji losing workers to Australia and New Zealand, while New Zealand also loses workers to Australia.”

He said the challenge was finding a balance that allowed Fiji to retain enough of its skilled workforce while building economic stability and prosperity domestically.

“So a degree of prosperity would come through with a low level of remittances.”

Fiji received $875.2 million in remittances in the year to June, a 26.3 per cent increase.

item.title: Robber accused denied bail
item.description: THREE men accused of violently attacking a Nadi taxidriver appeared before the Magistrate’s Court in Nadi yesterday facing aggravated robbery charges. Serupepeli Bogisa, Livai Nakaua, and Iliesa Buku appeared before Magistrate Talei Kean to face one count each of aggravated robbery.
item.content:encoded:
THREE men accused of violently attacking a Nadi taxidriver appeared before the Magistrate’s Court in Nadi yesterday facing aggravated robbery charges.

Serupepeli Bogisa, Livai Nakaua, and Iliesa Buku appeared before Magistrate Talei Kean to face one count each of aggravated robbery.

Police prosecutors allege that the trio jointly assaulted taxidriver Muni Sanjiv Mudaliar on August 25 in Nadi.

A video taken from the dashboard camera of the taxi showing two men allegedly involved in a robbery went viral after it was uploaded on social media.

During the brief court appearance, the police prosecutors strongly opposed bail for the accused persons because of the nature of the allegations and wider public interest.

Magistrate Kean ordered that all four be remanded in custody.

The matter has been transferred to the High Court in Lautoka and adjourned to September 11.

item.title: FIJI-AUSTRALIA BUSINESS COUNCIL I Kamikamica pushes deeper Fiji-Aust ties
item.description: FIJI is seeking to deepen its economic relationship with Australia, with the Government calling for greater investment, technology transfer and commercial partnerships as the Fiji-Australia Business Council marks its 40th anniversary. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Enterprise, Manoa Kamikamica, made the call while opening the Fiji-Australia and Australia-Fiji Business Forum yeste
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is seeking to deepen its economic relationship with Australia, with the Government calling for greater investment, technology transfer and commercial partnerships as the Fiji-Australia Business Council marks its 40th anniversary.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Enterprise, Manoa Kamikamica, made the call while opening the Fiji-Australia and Australia-Fiji Business Forum yesterday, where he said the longstanding “Vuvale” relationship should increasingly translate into investment, jobs and new business opportunities.

Mr Kamikamica said Fiji and Australia had built four decades of commercial relationships, people-to-people connections and institutional co-operation, but argued that the next phase of the relationship should go beyond traditional trade.

“We need to move from simply trading with each other to investing with each other, building with each other and growing with each other,” he said.

“Australia remains one of Fiji’s key trading and investment partners, with Australian-linked businesses already operating in sectors including tourism, financial services, telecommunications, manufacturing, renewable energy, infrastructure and professional services.

“The Government believes there is scope to expand that investment, particularly as Fiji pursues economic diversification and reforms aimed at making it easier for businesses to operate.”

Mr Kamikamica said the Investment Act 2021 had modernised Fiji’s investment framework by removing the former Foreign Investment Registration Certificate requirement, streamlining company incorporation and providing national treatment for foreign investors.

He also highlighted the establishment of the Investment Facilitation Committee, which brings together key Government agencies to address regulatory issues and facilitate major investment projects.

The committee is intended to help overcome challenges involving areas such as land, environment, utilities, immigration, planning and taxation.

He said the Government was also strengthening its Task Force on Investment Approval Process, with the aim of identifying delays and accelerating project implementation while maintaining legal and regulatory requirements.

Digital transformation was another major area identified for future investment.

Mr Kamikamica said Fiji’s National Digital Strategy was intended to support a more connected and innovation-driven economy, with opportunities emerging in cloud services, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, digital payments, e-commerce, data services and digital public infrastructure.

He pointed to growing international interest in Fiji’s digital economy, including Google’s entry into the country, as evidence of the potential for Fiji to become a regional platform for technology and digital services.

“The Government is also looking to attract investment into agriculture and agro-processing, with the Commercial Agriculture Taskforce addressing issues such as permits, biosecurity, environmental approvals and utility connections.

“The objective is to move agriculture further towards value-added and export-oriented production while creating stronger links between local producers and regional markets.”

Skills and labour mobility also featured in the Government’s investment agenda.

Mr Kamikamica announced that the Ministry of Immigration would streamline relevant work permit applications from the following Tuesday by removing five administrative requirements, including the tripartite agreement, advertising requirement, training plan and local understudy requirement.

He said the changes were intended to help businesses access specialised expertise while maintaining a longer-term focus on developing Fiji’s domestic workforce.

“We (Government) have identified tourism, agribusiness, ICT and business process outsourcing, manufacturing, logistics, maritime services, renewable energy and professional services among the sectors with investment potential.”

Mr Kamikamica also stressed the importance of ensuring that investment benefits Fiji’s small businesses and cooperatives through finance, technology, market access, skills development and participation in supply chains.

Looking ahead, he said Brisbane 2032 could provide additional opportunities for Fijian businesses in tourism, hospitality, logistics, food supply, creative industries and sports-related services.

He urged Australian companies to explore opportunities and partner with Fijian businesses, while challenging local enterprises to become more competitive, innovative and ready to meet international standards.

As the Fiji-Australia Business Council begins its next 40 years, the Government is positioning stronger trade and investment ties as a key part of Fiji’s broader economic ambitions.
